name: proxytunnel
desc: Create TCP tunnels through HTTPS proxies
why: Tunnels TCP through HTTPS proxies via CONNECT, a neat door into how proxies carry arbitrary traffic.

brief.what_it_is: proxytunnel is a command-line program that connects stdin and stdout to a server on the Internet by sending the traffic through an HTTPS proxy using the HTTP CONNECT method. It takes a destination host and port, plus optional proxy host, port, and credentials, and passes the bytes through as a tunnel. The README is written around using it as an SSH ProxyCommand, so SSH traffic travels through a corporate or other HTTP proxy. It also runs as an inetd service or a standalone daemon, and it supports SSL encryption, NTLM authentication, and chaining through a second proxy. The README says the version is 1.12.1.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it to reach his home machine over SSH from behind a proxy that only allowed HTTPS-style outbound traffic. The README says: "I originally wrote this program to be used as an extension to SSH, to be able to SSH to my box at home."
brief.how_it_works: The client connects to the HTTP proxy and sends a CONNECT request for the destination host:port, optionally with Proxy-Authorization credentials, and then relays stdin and stdout over the resulting connection. With -e or -E, the connection to the proxy or to the destination is wrapped in SSL, which helps when a proxy inspects protocol and rejects non-HTTPS traffic. The README says that in that case you need stunnel4 or a server that understands SSL on the other end.

commands_seen.context: Prints the built-in option list (version 1.12.1 is shown in the output).
Example line for ~/.ssh/config under a Host entry. It sends SSH through the proxy with SSL to the proxy, prompts for the password, and targets port 443 on the home box.
Final step once the ProxyCommand is set up; the README says "execute an 'ssh foobar' and you're in business!"

brief.install_notes: The README links to INSTALL.md for build instructions, which I did not fetch. Credentials can be given with -P on the command line (the password is then prompted for), with the PROXYPASS or PROXYUSER environment variables, with the HTTP_PROXY variable (format http://host:port/), or with a passfile (-F) containing proxy_user, proxy_passwd, remproxy_user, and remproxy_passwd. The server side needs sshd listening on 443 or 563 through an extra Port line in sshd_config, or a firewall redirect, because most HTTPS proxies allow only those ports. The README also mentions an Nginx, Apache, or Caddy setup, described in a linked blog post.
brief.standout: It reuses the ordinary HTTPS proxy CONNECT method as a generic byte pipe, so any TCP service, SSH being the main example, can get through a proxy that was built only for web traffic. The README is also a personal, first-person document from the original author, with a practical, hands-on tone.
brief.status: Status is unclear from the README alone. The version shown is 1.12.1, the copyright line says 2001-2024, and the README has no release date or commit date. The Travis CI badge points to travis-ci.org, which suggests older CI setup, and the README carries a 'maintainers wanted' badge, which suggests the project is looking for maintainers. I did not check the commit history, so this is not confirmed.
brief.caveats: Many corporate proxies filter traffic, so plain CONNECT tunnels may fail without -e or -E and extra server-side setup. The README warns that most HTTPS proxies only allow ports 443 and 563, so SSH has to be moved onto one of those. Self-signed certificates need -z, which turns off certificate verification. NTLM support needs -N, and the domain may need -t if autodetection fails. Build steps are in a separate INSTALL.md that I did not read, and the man page at docs/proxytunnel.1.adoc was not fetched either. The README does not state a license.
quotes: This is proxytunnel, a program that connects stdin and stdout to an origin server somewhere in the Internet through an industry standard HTTPS proxy.
I originally wrote this program to be used as an extension to SSH, to be able to SSH to my box at home.
Most HTTPS proxies do not allow access to ports other than 443 (HTTPS) and 563 (SNEWS), so some hacking is necessary to start the SSH daemon on the required port.
